USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Let the already-announced July 6 List 1 tariffs take effect and do not add new measures today. Keep the $200 billion list as unused contingent leverage, do not reopen the ZTE settlement as a bargaining chip, and leave a channel open for talks that address forced tech transfer and IP theft—not another purchase-only truce. Rolling back now would cash out pressure for nothing structural; firing the next tariff tranche before List 1 is even in force would convert a targeted 301 action into an open-ended farm-belt and inflation fight.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is only mildly elevated. The dispute is real and about to become operational: USTR locked a two-stage $50B plan (25% on ~$34B / 818 lines effective July 6; ~$16B later) and China announced matching 25% duties the same day, including soybeans, autos, and other politically sensitive U.S. exports, while voiding the May purchase understandings. That hits a sector already under stress—China bought about $14B of U.S. soy last year, futures fell to multi-year lows after the June 15/18 salvos, and farm-state Republicans (Grassley, Ernst, Reynolds) are warning a fragile ag economy will absorb the first blow. That is why the reading is above zero, not a clean opportunity. It is not a high or existential threat: U.S. industrial production is still rising, Michigan sentiment remains near 98, VIX is ~16, and private estimates put a $50B tariff package at roughly 0.1pp of GDP at most. The goods deficit and a jump in IMPCH (front-loading into July) show the real-economy bite has not arrived. CNY weakening (DEXCHUS ~6.64 on July 3 vs ~6.28 in late January) may partly offset U.S. duties and is a caution, not a crisis. Action stays at hold because May 19 already tested de-escalation: China offered to “significantly increase” purchases, Mnuchin called the war “on hold,” and ten days later the White House had to restart 301 because no structural IP remedy appeared. Early-June Ross–Liu talks then ended in impasse, with Beijing saying negotiated outcomes would lapse if tariffs proceeded. Escalating immediately to the June 18 $200B/10% identification would likely invite further calibrated retaliation and informal measures while U.S. 232 fights with allies already weaken the coalition around the 301 case. Conceding purchases or rolling back List 1 the day before implementation would confirm that a matching Chinese list is enough to break U.S. pressure. Hold the current posture: implement what is already teed up, measure the farm and price effects, and keep talks available for IP/tech-transfer commitments rather than another vague buy-more communiqué.
key_factors: July 6 List 1 ($34B at 25%) is locked and China has announced equal-scale retaliation the same day
May 19 purchase-only truce collapsed within 10 days; June Ross-Liu talks ended without a structural IP offer
Farm-belt exposure is the main U.S. cost: ~$14B soy to China, futures at multi-year lows, GOP farm-state pushback
U.S. macro still strong (IP up, sentiment ~98, small estimated GDP hit) so first-round tariffs are absorbable
Asymmetric remaining leverage via the unused $200B threat; further escalation now would spend it before List 1 is tested
CNY depreciation and import front-loading (IMPCH rising) already blunt/anticipate the tariff shock

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Implement the already-announced matching 25% tariffs on about $34B of U.S. goods (soybeans, other farm products, autos, aquatic products) when the U.S. List 1 duties take effect on 6 July. Do not add a new tariff tranche beyond the planned $16B second list, and do not open a fresh non-tariff front. Leave a channel for talks, but do not offer another standalone purchase package after the May joint statement was pocketed and then discarded.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. USTR’s Section 301 list is aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and machinery—the industrial-upgrading core—and List 1 (~$34B, 818 lines) is locked for 6 July, with List 2 (~$16B) behind it; Trump then directed USTR to identify another ~$200B at 10% if China answers the $50B action. That is a real hit to export-sector and tech-autonomy interests, and the April ZTE denial order showed Washington can threaten operational shutdown of a major firm via U.S. components. FX pressure is already visible: USD/CNY weakened through June into early July (spot ~6.64 on 3 July; monthly series 6.72), with a ~3.25% June slide and onshore/offshore prints through 6.7, while PBOC cut RRR to free ~700bn yuan of liquidity effective 5 July. This is not yet the +0.5 anchor: industrial production is still ~6% y/y, reserves remain ~$3.14tn with only a modest decline, the ZTE ban is being partially lifted after a $1bn fine/compliance deal, and U.S. goods imports from China were still rising into the summer (front-loading, not a collapse). Action should therefore be a mirror, not a widening. Unilateral purchase concessions were tried on 19 May (joint statement; Mnuchin called the war “on hold”) and the White House resumed 301 on 29 May—so further concede_purchases would buy nothing. Expanding beyond the announced like-for-like list would make the threatened $200B more likely and raise second-order costs for export hubs. Implementing the 15 June matching list (545 U.S. lines, ~$34B, 6 July) preserves credibility, concentrates pain on politically sensitive U.S. farm and auto exports, and keeps the option to talk once Washington has a reason to pause.
key_factors: U.S. List 1 25% on ~$34B Chinese goods effective 6 July; List 2 ~$16B pending
Trump 18 June instruction to identify ~$200B more at 10% if China retaliates
China already announced matching 25% on ~$34B U.S. soy, autos, farm and aquatic products for 6 July
May 19 purchase-truce collapsed on May 29 when the White House proceeded with 301
ZTE denial order (16 April) then settlement/partial lift — demonstrated U.S. component kill-switch, now being unwound at a price
Yuan slide and RRR cut show FX/growth stress, but IP ~6% and reserves ~$3.14tn mean this is not a financial-stability emergency
